idiom_name: domain collection type: private container + validating mutations + read-only exposure
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one type per domain collection (Orders, Roster, PriceList), keep the container a private member, and publish only three things - named mutations that validate the group's invariants (add/remove/clear, with an explicit replace-all for bulk loads), read access that cannot mutate the container (an unmodifiable view, a copy, a slice/span or an iterator), and the collection-level behaviour the domain needs (totals, selection, ordering). Validate in the constructor and in every mutator so no instance can exist in an illegal state, and answer the identity question - what makes two elements duplicates - inside the mutator. Keep traversal working with the language's own constructs by implementing its standard collection or iterator interface, and convert explicitly at framework boundaries where a plain list is required.
code_sketch:
class Orders:
    def __init__(self, items=()):
        self._items = tuple(items)   # private; never handed out
    def add(self, order): ...        # validates, returns new state
    def __iter__(self): yield from self._items
    def total(self): ...             # collection-level domain behaviour
# callers may iterate the collection but cannot add/remove behind its back
pitfalls: Publishing the container, or the structural methods of the underlying collection, leaves the invariants bypassable; expose only named operations and read-only traversal.
Two failure modes of exposure are equally wrong: a copy that callers think is live, and a view that callers think is a snapshot. State the semantics explicitly.
Skipping validation on bulk paths (addAll, replaceAll, hydration from the database) reintroduces exactly the illegal states the type exists to prevent.

Wrong move: subclass the framework's container to inherit iteration -> its full mutable API (add, remove, clear, sort) becomes your public surface and every invariant is bypassable -> instead wrap the container privately and implement only the iteration interface you mean to expose.

Wrong move: hand the lazy ORM collection straight across a service or transport boundary -> iterating it outside the unit of work initializes it late or detonates an N+1 query storm -> instead convert to a plain snapshot at the boundary or fetch-join the association before it leaves the session.

Wrong move: enforce uniqueness on the inverse side of a bidirectional association -> the collection's checks pass locally yet the framework persists only the owning side, so the mutation silently vanishes on flush -> instead mutate, and enforce, where the framework looks.
